findings.title: Rubric requires arguing PA fraud-in-inducement claims survive an integration clause, contrary to Yocca/Toy
findings.explanation: C-009 passes only if the motion argues that, under Pennsylvania law, a fraud claim based on pre-contract misrepresentations can survive an integration clause. It fails a brief that says integration clauses bar fraud claims. But the PA Supreme Court holds that in a fully integrated contract the parol evidence rule bars fraud-in-the-inducement claims; only fraud in the execution is excepted (Yocca; Toy; HCB). MSA §14.1 also has an express non-reliance clause, which Yocca treated as defeating justifiable reliance. So a candid brief that concedes the Yocca risk and pivots to the §5.1 warranty would fail C-008 and C-009. The alternative route, 'references the gist of the action doctrine', does not answer the integration clause at all: gist of the action is a separate defense Apex would raise, and eToll, one of the rubric's own examples, held fraud claims barred under it. The rubric therefore rewards a wrong statement of controlling law.

misstates it by claiming integration clauses bar all fraud claims under Pennsylvania law

findings.title: Reliance criteria aim at the minor reference-check issue and ignore the §14.1 non-reliance clause
findings.explanation: C-024 fails a motion that 'ignores the incomplete reference check problem' and treats that check as the main obstacle to justifiable reliance. Under Yocca, the obstacle that actually decides reliance is the express non-reliance acknowledgment in §14.1, and neither criterion mentions it. A competent brief could reasonably call the reference checks immaterial: Szymanski raised the gap on the 2/14 call and Bellingham answered it by naming Corridor Metals and PrimeTech. Such a brief could still be failed for not dwelling on the reference checks. The rubric steers toward a secondary issue and says nothing about the dispositive one.

findings.title: Example authorities for limitation-of-liability-vs-fraud are inapposite; Werwinski is adverse
findings.explanation: C-016 offers 'Walton v. Johnson' and 'Werwinski v. Ford Motor Co.' as Pennsylvania authority that limitation-of-liability clauses cannot shield fraud. Werwinski is a Third Circuit prediction that the economic loss doctrine bars intentional-fraud claims, which cuts against Ridgeline. Walton v. The solver never sees the examples, and the FAIL condition turns on stating the principle, so a correct answer is unlikely to fail. The defect is that a judge would credit a brief that miscites these cases.

findings.title: C-042 assumes contract damages are direct-only; §11.2 caps all theories, so the cap can reduce contract recovery
findings.explanation: C-042 fails a motion that 'suggests the LOL would reduce the contract damages', and it defines contract damages as the $2,007,500 in direct damages. C-054, however, has the motion claim consequential damages because the MSA has no waiver. If the contract claim carries consequential damages, contract-theory damages are $4,537,500. §11.2 caps aggregate liability 'whether in contract, tort ... or any other legal or equitable theory', so the cap would bring that down to $2,850,000. The rubric takes on the work-product memo's weak premise that the cap is 'silent on consequential damages'. A precise analysis saying the cap does limit total contract recovery could be failed.

findings.title: Requires citing the '12-month go-live' confidence statement, a forward-looking prediction a careful drafter may omit
findings.explanation: C-068 fails a motion that does not cite the proposal's statement that Apex was 'confident in delivering full go-live within 12 months'. That is a statement of confidence about future performance. Under the fraud rules, predictions and opinions are weak grounds for misrepresentation. The go-live date is also bound by contract under §3.4 and §3.5, so a breach argument does not need the proposal. A competent drafter might deliberately leave it out to keep the fraud theory on the provably false statements of existing fact (Teamcenter clients, AS9100D headcount). The instructions never ask for it.

blind.overall: Most of this rubric is well tied to the Ridgeline record: the caption, the damages arithmetic, the termination sequence, the evidence cites, and the Rule 56 statement coverage all check out against the documents. It has one serious legal defect. C-008 and C-009 require arguing that Pennsylvania fraud-in-the-inducement claims survive an integration clause, which contradicts Yocca and Toy, especially since MSA §14.1 has an express non-reliance clause. Because the headline metric is all-pass, a candid, correct brief could score zero on these two criteria alone. The record itself is badly contaminated: 11 of 17 files, including those named 'plaintiff-complaint' and 'statement-of-facts', come from an unrelated N.D. Ill. employment case, and no Ridgeline pleadings are supplied. Several other criteria are defensible but debatable. Some impose strategic choices as mandatory: punitive damages, the 12-month go-live statement, and the counterclaim. Others import weak premises from a work-product memo: the cap being 'silent' on consequential damages and a 'partly' causation qualifier that is not in the record. Fixing C-008 and C-009 and cleaning up the record would make the task largely sound.

sol_verdicts.reason: The contamination is real: 11 of 17 files are Huang v. Whitaker (N.D. Ill.). That is a document defect (my O2). But the caption criteria are supported by the record. email-and-slack-compilation gives 'Ridgeline Manufacturing Corp. v. Apex Digital Solutions, Inc., Case No. 2:23-cv-01487-NMR (W.D. Pa.)', and the instructions point to the contract and fraud case. Record citations (C-056) are generic and sound. C-055 is arguable only because of the 56.1 label and the N.D. Ill. template in the record (O8).

I agree, having read SodexoMAGIC at the source. Under Pennsylvania law a bare integration clause does not bar fraudulent inducement. Fraud-insulating language, meaning language that supersedes or disclaims prior representations, does. MSA §14.1 supersedes prior 'representations' and says each party 'has not relied upon any statement'. So the rubric requires arguing that the clause 'does not bar' the claims and fails a candid concession, which reverses the governing rule for this contract.

The label is wrong: W.D. Pa. uses a LCvR 56(B)(1) Concise Statement of Material Facts, not 'Local Rule 56.1'. The error starts in the instructions. C-055 tests only for a separate document with numbered paragraphs, which matches W.D. Pa. practice. A correctly titled statement should still pass, so this is unlikely to misgrade anything. It is a low-severity arguable defect, not a confirmed misgrade.

The instructions ask for a plaintiff's motion, so full advocacy is a fair default. Addressing Bellingham's 'overstated' testimony (C-014) and Apex's superior knowledge (C-026) are natural plaintiff arguments. C-007's pass condition requires counterclaim dismissal, but its fail condition covers only a missing conclusion, so a narrower prayer falls between the two (O7). C-024 pushes the reference-check issue and ignores the §14.1 non-reliance clause (O3).

findings.title: Rubric requires arguing fraud claims survive §14.1, but that clause is a PA fraud-insulating non-reliance clause
findings.explanation: C-008 requires arguing that the integration clause 'does not bar' the fraud claims. C-009 requires arguing that such claims 'can survive an integration clause', and it fails a brief that says the clause bars them. Pennsylvania draws a line here. Under SodexoMAGIC, reading Yocca and HCB, a bare integration clause does not bar fraudulent-inducement proof, but a clause that supersedes or disclaims prior representations does. MSA §14.1 supersedes all prior 'representations' and adds an express non-reliance acknowledgment. The MSA recitals also cover Apex's experience. A candid brief that concedes the parol-evidence and reliance bar and relies on the §5.1 warranties would fail C-008 and C-009. An overbroad 'Toy says fraud survives' argument would pass. The 'gist of the action' route in C-009 does not answer the integration question at all, and eToll applied that doctrine against the fraud plaintiff. Under all-pass scoring, this alone can zero a correct answer.

evidence.quote: supersedes all prior negotiations, representations, warranties, commitments, offers, and agreements, whether written or oral. Each Party acknowledges that it has not relied upon any statement, representation, promise, or agreement not expressly set forth in this Agreement
FAIL if the motion does not articulate this legal principle or misstates it by claiming integration clauses bar all fraud claims under Pennsylvania law.
preemptively argues why the integration clause does not bar those claims
Apex represents that it is an experienced ERP implementation services provider ... possesses the requisite skill, experience, personnel, and technical expertise

authorities.citation: SodexoMAGIC, LLC v. Drexel Univ., 24 F.4th 183 (3d Cir. 2022)
authorities.proposition: Under PA law, the parol evidence rule does not bar a fraudulent inducement claim where the integration clause lacks 'fraud-insulating provisions' such as language mentioning or disclaiming prior representations.

authorities.citation: Yocca v. Pittsburgh Steelers Sports, Inc., 854 A.2d 425 (Pa. 2004)
authorities.proposition: In a fully integrated contract disclaiming prior representations, parol evidence of fraudulent inducement is barred, and reliance on the superseded representations is not justifiable.

authorities.citation: Toy v. Metropolitan Life Ins. Co., 928 A.2d 186 (Pa. 2007)
authorities.proposition: Fraud in the execution, not fraud in the inducement, is the recognized exception to the parol evidence rule for integrated writings.

authorities.citation: eToll, Inc. v. Elias/Savion Advertising, Inc., 811 A.2d 10 (Pa. Super. 2002)
authorities.proposition: Gist of the action barred fraud claims tied to contract performance.

findings.suggested_fix: Pass a motion that recognizes §14.1 as a non-reliance and integration clause and responds reasonably. That could mean relying on the §5.1 and recital warranties, arguing a narrow exception, or candidly limiting the fraud request. Remove the requirement to argue the clause 'does not bar' the claims, and drop gist of the action as an alternative.

findings.suggested_fix: Make punitive damages optional, or pass a motion that reserves them for trial. Say 'factfinder' instead of 'jury'.

findings.title: Requires citing the proposal's '12-month go-live' confidence statement, a forward-looking prediction
findings.explanation: C-068 fails a motion that does not cite the proposal's statement that Apex was 'confident in delivering full go-live within 12 months'. That is a prediction or opinion, which is weak ground for fraud. The go-live date is already set by contract in MSA §3. A drafter might deliberately keep the fraud theory on false statements of existing fact. The instructions never ask for this statement.

evidence.quote: FAIL if this timeline commitment is not referenced.
Based on our proven methodology, we are confident in delivering full go-live within 12 months of project kickoff.

findings.suggested_fix: Drop C-068, or pass a motion that cites either the proposal's timeline or the MSA milestone dates.

findings.title: Witness names and facts are inconsistent across the Ridgeline documents
findings.explanation: The expert summary uses 'Derek Kresch', 'Diane Bellingham', 'Victoria Calloway', and 'James Hargrove'. The other documents use Jordan Kresch, Tara Bellingham, Margaret Calloway, and Dennis Hargrove. The Ostroff Slack message goes to 'Kevin Matsuda' in the deposition but includes 'Kevin Mallcroft' in the compilation. Teamcenter is version 13.2 in the MSA and 12.0 in the expert summary, and one email refers to 'six production facilities' where the record elsewhere has three. These are traps for the precise record citations that C-010, C-012, and C-061 require.

final.changes_from_blind:
1. O1 (C-008/C-009) is revised in its legal basis. I read SodexoMAGIC (3d Cir. 2022) at the source. It shows Pennsylvania law is more nuanced than my blind pass said: a bare integration clause does not bar fraudulent inducement, but fraud-insulating language that disclaims prior representations does. §14.1 is that kind of clause, so the criteria stay problematic, now on a sharper basis.
2. O2 (record contamination) no longer lists C-006, C-007, C-028, C-029, C-032, or C-055 as problematic. The counterclaim and punitive facts are in the record, even if thin, so those criteria now appear only in arguable findings (O7, O9). Sol's C-001 to C-003 are rejected because the caption facts are supported.
3. O3 drops C-026, since the superior-knowledge argument is a natural plaintiff argument.
4. O5 drops C-054, which states a true fact, and adds C-037, which shares the direct-only premise.
5. The blind counterclaim finding (old O9) now also covers C-007's gap between its pass and fail conditions. That point is adopted in part from Sol's B6-SJ-4, which I link to O3 and O7.
6. Renumbered: old O7 is now O9, old O8 is O10, old O9 is O7, and old O10 is O8.
7. Sol's C-014 point is rejected; addressing the 'overstated' testimony is fair to require.
final.overall: The rubric mostly tracks the Ridgeline record accurately: the caption, damages arithmetic, termination sequence, and evidence citations all check out. Its central legal defect is C-008 and C-009. They require arguing that fraud claims survive MSA §14.1, but under Pennsylvania law (SodexoMAGIC, Yocca) §14.1 is a fraud-insulating clause that supersedes prior representations and disclaims reliance on them. A candid, correct brief could therefore fail the all-pass metric on those two criteria alone. The record is badly contaminated: 11 of 17 files come from an unrelated N.D. Ill. employment case, and no Ridgeline pleadings are supplied, which also explains the 'Local Rule 56.1' mislabel. Several other criteria are arguable because they make strategic choices mandatory (counterclaim, punitive damages, the 12-month statement) or import weak work-product premises (the cap 'silent' on consequential damages, the 'partly' causation qualifier). Sol's core findings on contamination and the non-reliance clause match mine. I reject Sol's findings on the caption criteria, on C-014, and on C-026.
final.coverage: I read all 69 criteria and the instructions in the first pass, and re-read these 26 in this pass: C-001–003, 006–010, 012, 014–017, 024, 026–029, 032, 033, 037, 042, 054–056, 061, 068. In the first pass I read the six Ridgeline documents in full. In this pass I grepped the record for caption facts, the counterclaim, punitive damages, §14.1, the recitals, §11.2, the 'partly' qualifier, name inconsistencies, and the go-live quote. I read all of Sol's report files. SodexoMAGIC is verified on CourtListener in this pass; Yocca, Toy, Werwinski and Walton were verified in the first pass. W.D. Pa.
